title: Understanding the Real Estate Brokerage Act

chapters.title: Introduction
chapters.html:
In Quebec, real estate brokerage is governed by law and overseen by the OACIQ, whose mission is to protect the public. Understanding this framework means knowing your rights — whether you're buying or selling.

This guide explains the OACIQ's role, the protections you benefit from, and the documents and obligations that frame a transaction.

Informational content. Each chapter ends with a lined “My notes” page.

In Quebec, real estate brokerage is governed by law and overseen by the OACIQ, whose mission is to protect the public. This guide explains your rights: the OACIQ's role, your protections, the standardized contracts, the broker's duties and your recourses.

The through-line: knowing this framework means buying and selling knowing that you're protected.

chapters.title: The OACIQ and its mission
chapters.html:
Knowing who protects the public.

The Organisme d'autoréglementation du courtage immobilier du Québec (OACIQ) governs all the province's brokers: issuing and renewing licences, mandatory training, ethics, inspection and complaint handling.

Its primary mission is not to defend brokers, but to protect the public. Dealing with a broker holding a valid licence means benefiting from all this oversight — and from recourse mechanisms if something goes wrong.

  • Public register: each broker's licence can be checked online.
  • Mandatory continuing education to stay up to date.
  • A code of ethics governing professional conduct.

Concretely, the OACIQ issues licences, requires training, monitors practices and handles complaints. Checking your broker's licence in the public register takes thirty seconds and confirms that you're protected by all this oversight.

Emilie's tip

Before signing anything, type your broker's name into the OACIQ register. Thirty seconds that confirm the person is indeed authorized to represent you.

chapters.title: Your protections as a consumer
chapters.objective: Knowing the mechanisms that protect you.
chapters.html:
Knowing the mechanisms that protect you.

The law puts several safety nets in place, whether you're a buyer or a seller:

  • Standardized forms: governed contracts and declarations, the same for everyone.
  • The broker's duty to inform and verify.
  • Trust account: deposits are held in a protected account, separate from the broker's funds.
  • Compensation fund and insurance in the event of professional misconduct.

These protections govern the broker's conduct throughout the transaction, from the first meeting to signing at the notary.

These protections apply whether you're a buyer or a seller, and cover the whole course of the transaction — from the sums held in trust to compensation in the event of misconduct. They don't depend on your negotiating skill, but on the fact of going through a licensed broker.

Emilie's tip

Your protections don't depend on your negotiating skill: they're provided by law. But they only apply fully if you go through a licensed broker.

chapters.title: The standardized contracts of a transaction
chapters.html:
Understanding the governed documents.

A governed transaction relies on standardized contracts, designed to be fair and clear:

  • Brokerage contract (seller or buyer): defines the mandate and the fees.
  • Promise to purchase: the offer and its conditions.
  • Seller's declarations: what they know about the property.

The broker must verify certain information and advise you before you sign. Reading and understanding these documents isn't a formality: it's a right — and a good habit.

The standardized forms (brokerage contract, promise to purchase, declarations) are designed to be fair and clear. Take the time to read them: it's a right, and a good broker explains them clause by clause rather than rushing you to sign.

Emilie's tip

A good broker never has you sign “in a hurry”. They take the time to explain each clause. If you don't understand a passage, ask — that's exactly their role.

chapters.title: The broker's duties toward you
chapters.objective: Knowing what the law requires of them.
chapters.html:
Knowing what the law requires of them.

Beyond the forms, the broker is bound by specific professional obligations. Knowing them helps you recognize good support — and react if something is off.

  • Duty to advise: to inform you objectively, even when the truth is unwelcome.
  • Verification: to validate information before circulating it.
  • Disclosure: to reveal any factor that could affect your decision (including a conflict of interest).
  • Fair treatment of the parties to the transaction.

These duties exist whether or not the broker represents you directly: the law protects the public as a whole.

The duty to advise requires the broker to inform you objectively, to verify before circulating, to disclose any conflict of interest and to treat the parties fairly. Be wary of a broker who pushes you to decide quickly or downplays a defect: that's exactly the opposite of their role.

Emilie's tip

Be wary of a broker who pushes you to decide quickly or downplays a defect. The duty to advise is precisely about telling you what you need to hear, not just what pleases you.

chapters.title: If there's a problem: your recourses
chapters.html:
Knowing the avenues of recourse.

If a dispute arises, you're not alone. Several recourses exist, graduated by seriousness:

  1. Talk about it first with the broker and their agency: many misunderstandings are settled there.
  2. OACIQ assistance: information and support for the public.
  3. A formal complaint to the syndic in the event of an ethical breach.
  4. Compensation possible through the fund provided in the event of fraud or serious misconduct.

Keep all your documents and written exchanges: they're precious if you have to assert your rights.

In the event of a dispute, the recourses are graduated: talk about it first with the broker and their agency, then OACIQ assistance, a complaint to the syndic, and compensation in the event of serious misconduct. Keep all your documents and written exchanges: they're what make the proof.

Emilie's tip

Keep a written record of everything: emails, signed forms, meeting notes. In the event of a dispute, it's these documents that make the difference, not memories.

chapters.title: Action plan
chapters.html:
Your next steps, concretely.

This week

  1. Check the broker's licence in the OACIQ register.
  2. Learn about my consumer rights.

Within 30 days

  1. Read the contracts carefully before signing.
  2. Keep a copy of all the documents.

Next

  1. Know that the OACIQ is there in the event of a problem.

Useful reflexes

  1. Check my broker's licence in the OACIQ register.
  2. Read each contract before signing and keep all my copies.

chapters.title: Resources & glossary
chapters.html:
• OACIQ: the body that governs brokerage and protects the public.
  • Brokerage licence: to be checked in the OACIQ register.
  • Trust account: a protected account where deposit sums are held.
  • Brokerage contract: a governed agreement between client and broker.
  • Duty to advise: the obligation to inform and advise the client.
  • OACIQ: the body that governs brokerage and protects the public.
  • Trust account: a protected account where deposit sums are held.
  • Duty to advise: the obligation to inform and advise objectively.
  • Syndic: the body that receives ethics complaints.
  • Compensation fund: protection in the event of fraud or serious misconduct.
